say.text: Two cases on your ward round. Case X: pain when you extend the right hip. Case Y: pain when you rotate the flexed right hip inwards.
Which case suggests a retrocaecal appendix?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Extending the hip stretches the psoas, and a retrocaecal appendix lies on it, so pain appears on extension.
Retrocaecal is the commonest position of the appendix, which is why this sign matters most.
Tempting: both signs are right-hip tests, so it feels natural to pair the second case with the position you learned first.
But internal rotation of the flexed hip loads the obturator internus, which a pelvic appendix touches. That pairs Case Y with the pelvic position (K39, K93).
What is right: Case X is extension, the psoas and the retrocaecal appendix. Pair each sign with the muscle it stresses.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair the signs by muscle: psoas with extension and retrocaecal; obturator with internal rotation and pelvic.

say.text: Ask which muscle each movement stretches. Then ask which part of the caecum or pelvis lies against that muscle.
Your registrar says: 'For the psoas sign you flex the right hip and rotate it inwards.'
Which correction is right?

choices.label: You're right: flexed internal rotation is the psoas test
Psoas needs hip extension; flexed internal rotation is obturator
Both are the same hip test, so either name will do
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Extending the right hip stretches the psoas. Flexing it and rotating it inwards tenses the obturator internus.
Each name belongs to one movement, so keep the two apart by the muscle each one stresses.
Tempting: both are right-hip manoeuvres that hurt in the same lower abdomen, so the names feel swappable.
But flexing and rotating the hip inwards tests the obturator, not the psoas. The psoas sign needs the hip extended (K38, K39).
What is right: psoas is extension; obturator is flexion with internal rotation. The movement sets the name (K106).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the movement first: extension is psoas, internal rotation of the flexed hip is obturator.

say.text: Tempting: both signs are pain-on-movement tests of the same joint, so they can feel like one manoeuvre with two labels.
But each one stresses a different muscle. The psoas is stretched by extension; the obturator internus is tensed by internal rotation of a flexed hip (K38, K39).
What is right: learn one movement per name. They are two signs, each with its own muscle (K106).

sure_note.text: You were sure the two are one test. They stress different muscles, so they are two signs.

say.text: Ask what extending the hip stretches, and what internally rotating a flexed hip tenses.
A surgeon says: 'The appendix gangrenes first, and the lumen blocks only later.'
Which correction is right?

choices.label: Pain localises to the right iliac fossa first, then the umbilicus
The lumen blocks first; rising pressure then cuts the artery supply
Ischaemia starts before any blockage, and the lumen blocks afterwards
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Obstruction raises intraluminal pressure, venous congestion follows, and the end-artery supply then fails (K24, K25).
The appendicular artery is an end artery, so ischaemia leads to gangrene and then perforation, at the end of the chain (K4).
Tempting: pain is the first thing the patient describes, so it feels like the first event in the chain.
But early pain is visceral and periumbilical, from the T10 supply. It moves to the right iliac fossa only when the parietal peritoneum is involved (K26, K27).
What is right: the lumen blocks first, pressure rises, and only then the pain localises to the right iliac fossa (K5, K24).

sure_note.text: You were sure the pain localises first. It starts periumbilical and shifts to the right iliac fossa later (K5, K27).

say.text: Tempting: gangrene is the feared end, so the picture of a dying appendix feels like the opening event.
But the artery fails because rising pressure compresses it. Ischaemia sits downstream of the blockage, so it cannot come first (K24, K25).
What is right: obstruction, rising pressure, venous congestion, arterial compromise, then gangrene and perforation (K24, K25).

sure_note.text: You were sure ischaemia came first. The lumen blocks first, and pressure cuts the end-artery supply afterwards (K25).

say.text: Start with what blocks the lumen. Then ask what raised pressure does to venous flow, and then to arterial flow.
A patient has right iliac fossa tenderness, rebound tenderness, leucocytosis, fever, anorexia and nausea. He has no migration of pain and no left shift.
What is his Alvarado total?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Right iliac fossa tenderness and leucocytosis score 2 each; rebound, fever, anorexia and nausea score 1 each (K7, K107).
Two 2-point items plus four 1-point items give 8. A score of 7 or more makes appendicitis likely (K47).
Tempting: rebound tenderness is a peritoneal sign, so it feels as if it deserves the top weight alongside tenderness.
But only right iliac fossa tenderness and leucocytosis score 2. Rebound scores 1, so a total of 9 overcounts (K107, K7).
What is right: two 2-point items plus four 1-point items give 8. Count the weights, not the feel of each sign.

sure_note.text: You were sure rebound scores 2. The table gives it 1; only tenderness and leucocytosis take 2 (K107).

say.text: Tempting: leucocytosis is a laboratory result, so it feels like a minor item next to the clinical signs.
But leucocytosis scores 2, the same as right iliac fossa tenderness. Scoring it 1 drops the total to 7 and understates the risk (K107).
What is right: two 2-point items and four 1-point items total 8 (K7).

sure_note.text: You were sure leucocytosis scores 1. In the Alvarado table it scores 2, like tenderness (K107).

say.text: Score the items in pairs: which two carry 2 points, and what does every other item carry?
A house officer says: 'Ultrasound is the investigation of choice in every adult, so a negative scan ends the work-up.'
Which reply is right?

choices.label: Ultrasound is the investigation of choice for all ages, as old keys say
A negative scan in an adult is decisive, so the patient can go home
CT is most accurate in adults; a negative scan does not exclude appendicitis

say.text: Yes. CT is the most accurate test in adults, and ultrasound is first only in children and pregnancy (K99, K98).
A negative ultrasound in an adult does not close the question, so the work-up goes on to CT (K55).
Tempting: ultrasound is the test named in most past-paper stems, so it feels like the answer for everyone.
But the old key expected ultrasound as the investigation of choice in general (K108). That key does not describe adults, where CT is the most accurate test (K99).
What is right: teach both. PYQs expected ultrasound in general; current practice uses it first in children and pregnancy, and CT for adults (K98).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the age: the ultrasound key fits children and pregnancy, not adults (K98).

say.text: Tempting: a scan that shows nothing feels reassuring, and the ultrasound is the test you ordered.
But in an adult a negative ultrasound does not exclude appendicitis. CT has the highest sensitivity and specificity (K55).
What is right: a negative ultrasound in an adult leads to contrast CT, not to discharge (K55, K99).

sure_note.text: You were sure a negative scan is decisive in an adult. It is not; CT is the test that settles it (K55).

say.text: A 9-year-old boy and a 31-year-old pregnant woman at 24 weeks both have right iliac fossa pain.
Which first imaging is right for each?

choices.label: Contrast CT for both, since CT is the most accurate test
Ultrasound for the boy, MRI for the woman

say.text: Yes. Ultrasound is the first test in children and in pregnancy, as graded compression (K98, K54).
Pregnancy keeps the same first rung. MRI is added only if ultrasound is inconclusive (K56).
Tempting: CT is the most accurate test, so it feels like the safest choice for any patient with right iliac fossa pain.
But accuracy is not the first question. Children and pregnant women get ultrasound first; CT is the adult test (K98, K99).
What is right: ultrasound first for both the boy and the pregnant woman (K98).

sure_note.text: You were sure CT is right. Children and pregnant women start with ultrasound, whatever the accuracy (K98).

say.text: Tempting: MRI avoids radiation and is very accurate, so it feels like the best first test in pregnancy.
But MRI is the second rung, used when ultrasound is inconclusive, not the first (K56, K100).
What is right: ultrasound first for the pregnant woman and for the boy; MRI only if ultrasound fails (K98, K100).

sure_note.text: You were sure MRI comes first in pregnancy. The first rung is ultrasound; MRI follows an inconclusive scan (K100).

say.text: A 26-year-old woman has right iliac fossa pain and a late period. She reaches casualty.
What is your first step?

choices.label: Contrast CT now; the pregnancy test can follow
Serum or urine beta-hCG before any scan or theatre
Diagnostic laparoscopy at once; it answers both questions

say.text: Yes. Every woman of reproductive age needs a beta-hCG, because ectopic pregnancy changes the imaging and the operation (K53, K59).
The pregnancy test comes before the scan or theatre, not after the appendix looks normal (K53).
Tempting: the appendix is the likely cause, so imaging it now feels like the efficient step.
But a scan before beta-hCG can miss an ectopic pregnancy, which changes the whole plan (K53, K59).
What is right: beta-hCG first, then imaging or surgery as the findings direct (K53).

sure_note.text: You were sure imaging comes first. The pregnancy test changes everything, so it goes first (K53).

say.text: Tempting: laparoscopy both looks and treats, so it feels like one efficient step that answers both questions.
But operating before excluding pregnancy risks a wrong operation for an ectopic pregnancy (K59, K53).
What is right: beta-hCG first, then imaging or theatre, depending on the result (K53).

sure_note.text: You were sure one operation answers everything. The pregnancy test comes first, every time (K53).

say.text: Two adults have CT-proven appendicitis. Patient A has uncomplicated disease with no appendicolith. Patient B is the same but has an appendicolith.
Which patient is a candidate for antibiotics-first?

choices.label: Patient B, since antibiotics-first now applies to every CT-proven case
Patient A, the one without an appendicolith
Neither: appendicectomy is the only treatment for both

say.text: Yes. Antibiotics-first is accepted for selected adults with CT-proven uncomplicated disease (K71).
An appendicolith predicts failure and a higher perforation risk, so it moves the patient to surgery (K15, K71).
Tempting: CT has confirmed appendicitis, and antibiotics-first is now mentioned as an option, so the label feels like it fits.
But the appendicolith is an exclusion. It predicts antibiotic failure, so it takes the patient off the non-operative pathway (K71, K15).
What is right: antibiotics-first suits uncomplicated disease without an appendicolith, which is Patient A (K12, K71).

sure_note.text: You were sure Patient B qualifies. The appendicolith is the qualifier that excludes antibiotics-first (K71).

say.text: Tempting: appendicectomy is the treatment of choice in every past-paper answer, so 'only' feels fair.
But treatment of choice is not the only treatment. Current practice accepts antibiotics-first for selected CT-proven uncomplicated adults (K110, K9).
What is right: appendicectomy stays the default; antibiotics-first is an option for selected patients (K9, K110).

sure_note.text: You were sure appendicectomy is the only option. The old key said so, but current practice accepts antibiotics-first in selected patients (K110).

say.text: Two patients. A has five days of right iliac fossa pain, a tender stable mass and low-grade fever. B has swinging fever and a drainable collection on CT.
Which pair of actions is right?

choices.label: A: immediate appendicectomy; B: image-guided drainage with antibiotics
A: Ochsner-Sherren regimen; B: image-guided drainage with antibiotics
A: Ochsner-Sherren regimen; B: laparotomy and open drainage

say.text: Yes. A stable appendicular mass is treated by the Ochsner-Sherren regimen; a drainable abscess by image-guided drainage with antibiotics (K73, K76).
The regimen is stopped and surgery done if pulse, pain or mass size worsens, or peritonitis spreads (K74).
Tempting: a tender mass and five days of pain feel like a reason to remove the appendix at once.
But a stable appendicular mass is first treated conservatively. Early surgery is reserved for a regimen that fails (K73, K74).
What is right: the regimen for the mass, and image-guided drainage for the drainable collection (K73, K103).

sure_note.text: You were sure surgery is right for a mass. The regimen comes first, and surgery follows its failure (K74).

say.text: Tempting: open drainage feels definitive when the collection is large, so laparotomy looks thorough.
But percutaneous image-guided drainage is first-line for a drainable abscess. Open drainage is the fallback when it fails or is unavailable (K76, K103).
What is right: image-guided drainage with antibiotics for Patient B (K103).

sure_note.text: You were sure open drainage is right. Image-guided drainage is first-line; open drainage is the fallback (K76).

say.text: A 58-year-old man's appendicular mass has resolved on the regimen.
What is your next step?

choices.label: Routine interval appendicectomy at six to eight weeks, as the old key says
Colonoscopy or CT to exclude caecal carcinoma, then decide on surgery
Immediate appendicectomy, since the mass proves the appendix is diseased

say.text: Yes. Interval surgery is now selective, and an older patient needs colonoscopy or CT to exclude caecal carcinoma (K75).
Decide on surgery after the work-up, not from the calendar (K75).
Tempting: interval appendicectomy at six to eight weeks is the classic answer, so it feels like the routine.
But that was the PYQ expectation. Current practice makes interval surgery selective and checks older patients first (K109, K75).
What is right: for a 58-year-old, exclude caecal carcinoma first, then decide on surgery (K75).

sure_note.text: You were sure the calendar decides. The routine is now selective, with work-up in older patients (K109).

say.text: Tempting: the mass proves the appendix is diseased, so removing it now feels like the logical step.
But the mass has resolved on the regimen, so immediate surgery is not indicated. Surgery follows a failing regimen (K73, K74).
What is right: work-up for caecal carcinoma first, then a selective decision on interval surgery (K75).

sure_note.text: You were sure a mass means immediate surgery. A resolved mass is managed by work-up and selection (K75).

say.text: Two patients. A is ten days after open appendicectomy, with faecal discharge from the wound and a slipped stump. B is two days into a stay, with perforation and peritonitis before theatre.
Which patient has a complication of the operation?

choices.label: Patient B, as peritonitis is the complication of the surgical episode
Patient A, with a faecal fistula from the stump

say.text: Yes. A faecal fistula can follow a slipped stump ligature, so it is a complication of the operation (K84).
Perforation with peritonitis is a complication of the disease itself, before any operation (K78).
Tempting: peritonitis is the dramatic outcome of the whole episode, so it feels like a complication of the surgery too.
But perforation with generalised peritonitis comes from the disease, before theatre. Merging the two complication lists is the error (K78, K82).
What is right: disease complications are perforation, mass, abscess and pylephlebitis; operative ones are wound infection, fistula and stump problems (K80, K84).

sure_note.text: You were sure perforation is an operative complication. It is a disease complication, and it can happen before theatre (K78).

say.text: A histology report after appendicectomy is read in the teaching round.
Which is the most common tumour of the appendix?

choices.label: Adenocarcinoma, since it is the most serious

say.text: Yes. Carcinoid, the neuroendocrine tumour, is the commonest appendix tumour and usually sits at the tip (K105, K89).
PYQs expected under 2 cm at the tip to need appendicectomy alone, and over 2 cm to need right hemicolectomy (K111).
Tempting: a mucocele is a familiar appendix lesion, and its name sounds like the answer for a frequent finding.
But a mucocele can rupture and cause pseudomyxoma peritonei. It is a complication to recognise, not the commonest tumour (K90).
What is right: carcinoid is the commonest appendix tumour, usually at the tip (K105).

sure_note.text: You were sure a mucocele is the commonest. The commonest is carcinoid; the mucocele is a risk of rupture (K90).

say.text: Tempting: the tumour that sounds most serious feels like the one an exam would call most common.
But severity and frequency are different questions. Carcinoid, not adenocarcinoma, is the commonest appendix tumour (K105).
What is right: carcinoid, usually at the tip, is the commonest; the size rule then decides surgery (K105, K111).

sure_note.text: You were sure the most serious-sounding tumour is the commonest. Frequency and severity are separate (K105).
